<meta>This page contains verses 498 to 507 of the Therigatha, specifically from the verses attributed to Sumedha. The text uses metaphors to illustrate the vastness of suffering in the cycle of rebirth and the dangers of sensual pleasures.</meta>

# VERSES OF THE ELDER NUNS

Remember that in the beginningless <term>samsara</term> <gloss>cycle of birth and death</gloss>, if the earth of the Rose-apple Island <note>original: "Jambudipa", referring to the Indian subcontinent or the known world</note> were rolled into little balls the size of jujube stones, they would not be enough to represent all the mothers and fathers one has had. 498.

Remember that if all the grass, wood, branches, and leaves were gathered from the beginningless cycle and cut into finger-length pieces, they would not be enough to represent all the fathers and grandfathers one has had. 499.

Remember the blind turtle in the eastern ocean and the yoke-hole in the western ocean; the chance of the turtle putting its head through that hole is the comparison used for the rarity of obtaining a human birth. 500.

Remember that the physical form is like a lump of foam, a body of misery and without substance; look at the <term>khandhas</term> <gloss>aggregates of existence</gloss> as impermanent, and remember the many afflictions in the hells. 501.

Remember those who fill up the cemeteries again and again in various births; remember the fears of the crocodiles <note>a metaphor for the dangers of the world</note>, and remember the Four Noble Truths. 502.

While the Deathless <note>Nirvana</note> exists, why do you drink the five bitter things? For all sensual delights are more bitter than those five bitter medicines. 503.

While the Deathless exists, what use to you are sensual pleasures which are burning fevers? For all sensual delights are blazing, boiling, disturbed, and inflamed. 504.

While there is a state of no enmity, what use to you are sensual pleasures which have many enemies? Sensual pleasures are shared with kings, fire, thieves, water, and unloved heirs; they have many enemies. 505.

While liberation exists, what use to you are sensual pleasures which involve execution and imprisonment? For in sensual pleasures there is execution and imprisonment; those who crave sensual pleasures experience many sufferings. 506.

A grass torch, when lit, burns the one who holds it if they do not let go; sensual pleasures are like that torch, they burn those who do not let go of them. 507.

Do not, for the sake of a small amount of sensual happiness, abandon a vast happiness.

Do not be like a broad-finned fish that swallows the hook and is later destroyed. <note>The broad-finned fish is a traditional metaphor for one who is lured by sensory pleasure only to find it leads to suffering.</note> Restrain yourself from sensual desires, or they will treat you like a dog bound by a chain. Indeed, these desires will devour you just as the <term>Candala</term> <gloss>outcastes</gloss> treat a hungry dog.

You will experience immeasurable suffering and many mental distresses if you remain attached to sensual pleasures. Renounce these unstable desires. Since the ageless state exists, what use have you for these pleasures that are subject to decay? All births, in all places, are seized by death and disease.

This <note>the state of Nibbana</note> is ageless; this is undying; this is the ageless and undying state that is free from sorrow. It is without enemies, without confinement, without stumbling, without fear, and without affliction. This deathless state has been attained by many and can still be obtained today by one who applies themselves with thorough attention <note>original: <term>yoniso</term></note>. But it cannot be reached by one who does not strive.

Thus spoke Sumedha, finding no delight in conditioned things. While Anikaratta <note>the prince who wished to marry her</note> was pleading with her, Sumedha cut off her hair and threw it on the ground. <note>Cutting the hair is a symbolic act of renouncing worldly life and beauty to become a nun.</note>

Anikaratta stood up and, with hands pressed together in respect, begged her father: "Let Sumedha go, so that she may go forth into the homeless life to see the truth of liberation."

Released by her mother and father, she went forth into the homeless life, fearing sorrow and danger. While still a student, she realized the six higher powers <note>original: <term>abhiññā</term></note> and reached the highest fruit <note>Arahantship, or full enlightenment</note>.

Marvelous and wonderful was the <term>Nibbana</term> <gloss>extinction of suffering</gloss> of that princess. In her final hour, she explained her conduct in previous lives:

"In the time of the Blessed One Konagamana <note>a Buddha of a previous age</note>, in a newly built monastery, three of us friends gave the gift of a dwelling place. Ten times, a hundred times, a thousand times, and ten thousand times we were reborn among the gods. What need is there to mention our births among humans? Among the gods, we possessed great psychic power. What need is there to mention our status among humans?"

<summary>The nun Sumedha rejects a royal marriage, cuts her hair in renunciation, and achieves enlightenment. She recounts her past merit of donating a monastery during the time of a previous Buddha.</summary>
<keywords>Sumedha, Therigatha, renunciation, Nibbana, Konagamana Buddha, merit, rebirth</keywords>

I was the woman-treasure, the chief queen of the Lord of the Seven Treasures <note>original: "Sattaratanassa mahesī itthiratanam ahaṃ āsi." This refers to the consort of a Universal Monarch or Cakkavatti.</note>. 520.
That was the cause, that was the source, that was the root: patience in the teaching of the Teacher. That was the first meeting; that was the Nirvana for one delighted in the Dhamma. 521.
Thus they speak, those who have faith in the word of the One of Supreme Wisdom. They grow weary of existence; having grown weary, they become dispassionate. 522.

She spoke these verses. There, in the city of Mantāvatī <note>original: "Mantāvatiyā nagare"</note> means in the city named Mantāvatī. Of King Koñca <note>original: "Rañño Koñcassa"</note> means she was the daughter born from the womb of the chief queen of the king named Koñca. By name, she was Sumedhā. Pleasing through the practitioners of the teaching <note>original: "Pāsādikā sāsanakārehī"</note> means she was one who had gained confidence in the Triple Gem through the noble ones who practice the Teacher's instruction and through the preaching of the Dhamma.

Virtuous <note>original: "Silavatī"</note> means endowed with conduct and morality. Eloquent <note>original: "Cittakathā"</note> means her talk on the Dhamma was variegated and beautiful. Learned <note>original: "Bahussutā"</note> means she was well-established in the scriptures. Disciplined in the Buddha's teaching <note>original: "Buddhasāsane vinītā"</note> means she was disciplined in the teaching of the Buddhas because her defilements were removed through wise attention following the discourses, understanding how one goes forth, how one attains Nirvana, and what constitutes morality, concentration, and wisdom. Her body, speech, and mind were restrained. Listen, both of you <note>original: "Ubhayo nisāmethā"</note> means you two should listen to my words. The construction is: she spoke having approached her mother and father.

Even if it is divine <note>original: "Yadi pi dibbaṃ"</note> means even that which belongs to the heavenly worlds, everything included in existence, is impermanent, unstable, suffering, and subject to change. How much more so the empty sensual pleasures? <note>original: "Kim aṅgaṃ pana tucchā kāmā"</note> means how much more so are human pleasures? Because they are essentially unpleasant, they are empty and hollow. They are like a drop of honey on the edge of a sword, providing little taste but resulting in great suffering and much distress now and in the future.

Bitter <note>original: "Kaṭukā"</note> means undesirable; they are like venomous snakes because of their fearful nature. Infatuated with which pleasures <note>original: "Yesu kāmesu mucchitā"</note> means those who are stuck in them. It is ingrained in human nature to desire many things, a desire that cannot be satisfied except through the knowledge of new things and, as follows from this, through admiration and inquiry. Thus, we neglect what is common and obvious, while new and distant things please us. In order for men not alien to letters to satisfy this, without turning the love of learning into idle curiosity—which sometimes examines things whose knowledge is of little use—they adopted this caution: to mix the useful with the sweet and the sweet with the useful, and to select the subjects of their Academic discourses, singular in both their utility and their rarity. In this part, they imitate the Emperor in § 3 of the Preface to the Institutes, who thought the minds of students should be led from ancient fables to more weighty and useful matters. Following them, I have decided for this time to offer a certain tasting of the theme of **ALTERO TANTO** <gloss>the other as much/double</gloss>, which commends itself sufficiently by its rarity and utility, and to reserve a fuller treatment of the same for another time. May it be so with the help of God.

3. Various meanings of this are found in our law: 1. It is taken broadly for any thing’s "other as much" or "other as many." In the aforementioned *Law 13, ff. de liber. et posth.*, where the inheritance is divided into seven parts according to the will, Julian says the son of the testator will have "as much again" more than the wife; likewise, the wife "as much again" more than the daughter. And thus the son received four parts, the wife two, the daughter one. That is, the son to the mother, and the mother to the daughter, were in double proportion, as Gothofredus notes on that very *Law 13*, which is called here "the other as much," and here it concerns the division of an inheritance. 2. Strictly for that double amount which is exacted in the name of a penalty, interest, or some accession. 3. Most strictly, with respect to only that accession which, in a loan, has proceeded up to the sum of the principal, which is what we shall mainly address in our inquiry.

4. With this meaning, I define "the other as much" as nothing other than such an accession, or as much of an accession, added to the principal given in a loan, as the principal sum itself is.

5. Since it is so arranged in a loan that usury agrees with the principal in regard to its matter (Hotoman, *de usur.* c. 2), and an accession of a different kind than the principal is not, strictly speaking, usury, but something given or promised in place of usury (*Law 14, 17, C. de usur.*), I have therefore said that the "other as much" agrees with the principal in quality.

For as soon as something is given for the sake of an accession beyond "as much again," it is no longer the "other as much," but begins to be the "third as much," if I may speak in this way. Just as it cannot be called "as much" below the equalization of the simple or principal amount, since it has not yet reached that quantity, nor is it "as much" as the principal itself is.

7. As for the opinion of Bartolus, Baldus, Castrensis, and others, who believe that *when it is said in law that usury should not exceed the double, it is understood as usury of one year*, it is easy to conjecture that nothing is more absurd, as *Fachin. 10, controversy 65* relates. For it cannot happen in such a short space of time, unless by a cruel creditor, that as much is exacted in the name of usury (for example, in a single year) as the principal debt is worth. Nor is the "other as much" or "double" considered if it consists of a smaller or not equal quantity to the principal, as has been said before.

8. Hence the controversy is declared, which holds almost the first place in this matter: Does the "simple" exist within the "other as much"? And although *Budaeus on Law 10, Code de usuris*, wished that the "simple" does not exist in this double of usury, and thus usury could run up to the double of the principal, the principal not being computed—*Molinaeus, treatise on usury, number 47*.

The sons of the Gods use the word Fluor broadly for every flux or falling away of peccant matter, from any part and to any part. Strictly and specifically, however, it also denotes Catarrh, or the preternatural flowing down of vicious matter collected in the head into the underlying parts. ## II.

Regarding synonymy, our condition acquires various other names. Hippocrates and Galen—the former indeed in *On the Nature of Woman*, Section XV, text II, and Section XLV, text I; the latter in Book III of *On the Causes of Symptoms*, and also in *On the Difference of Symptoms* and VI *On Affected Parts*—call it *rhoon* or *rhoun gynaikeion*, a flux or female fluor, perhaps because it is proper to women. In Forestus, *Observations*, Book XVIII, Observation XIX, it is called a Female Profluvium, White Superfluity, White Flowers, Female Purgation, and so forth, the reason for which denomination is clear from the words themselves. Riverius, in *Medical Practice*, Book XV, chapter IV, chose to name it a Profluvium of the Uterus. The most sagacious investigator of Nature, Gualtherus Charleton, preferred to call it Rheumatism of the Uterus. In Sylvius, *Medical Practice*, Book III, chapter IV, because of the similarity it seems to have at first glance with phlegm, it is called Phlegmatic Humor. It is also given the title by some of White Menses; but since this fluor is accustomed to be amiss more frequently outside the flux of the months, before or after the Natural Lunar Tribute has been paid, than during the menstrual time itself, with the most accurate Sylvius, we do not see why it deserves this name, except most improperly. To the Germans, it is usually called *der weisse Fluß*, and so forth; and who could recount all the names devised by so many physicians and imposed upon this condition?

Since, therefore, the uterus exists as the cause not only of this, but of all diseases (that is to say, female ones) according to the divine Coan <note>referring to Hippocrates</note>, and when the uterus is affected, the whole body is drawn into its *koinonia* (communion) and contagion, I think I shall not stray from the goal if, before I proceed to the rest, I have inquired with the strength of my small talent, briefly and in three words, into its position, magnitude, figure, substance, and connection; and a little more accurately, though still briefly, into the vessels, so that I may more happily attain the proposed end.

->VI.<-

The Position of the uterus immediately reveals a singular divine providence, while we see it placed in the hypogastrium, or the lowest part of the abdomen, between the bladder and the rectum, which are for it like two cushions, lest the tender embryo be injured by the hardness of the bones. Furthermore, that place is also most suitable not only for the growth of the conceived fetus—since when the uterus is distended into a huge mass in the final months, more space was required—but also for its exclusion once perfected.
